Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)

Let \(M_d=\max A_d\). First note that taking \(i=j\) gives

\[
|A_i|=|A_i\cap A_i|=\gcd(i,i)=i.
\]

So in particular \(|A_1|=1,\ |A_{250}|=250\), hence

\[
M_1\ge 1,\qquad M_{250}\ge 250.
\]

We will use the following simple lemma.

**Lemma.** If \(X,Y\) are finite nonempty sets of positive integers, then

\[
\max X+\max Y\ge |X\cup Y|+\min(|X|,|Y|).
\]

Indeed, let \(M=\max(\max X,\max Y)\) and \(m=\min(\max X,\max Y)\). Since \(X\cup Y\subseteq \{1,2,\dots,M\}\), we have \(M\ge |X\cup Y|\). Also \(m\) is the maximum of either \(X\) or \(Y\), so \(m\) is at least the size of that set, hence \(m\ge \min(|X|,|Y|)\). The lemma follows.

Now apply the lemma to pairs of the relevant sets.

1. For \(A_2\) and \(A_5\),

\[
|A_2|=2,\quad |A_5|=5,\quad |A_2\cap A_5|=\gcd(2,5)=1,
\]

so

\[
M_2+M_5\ge |A_2\cup A_5|+\min(2,5)=(2+5-1)+2=8.
\]

2. For \(A_{10}\) and \(A_{25}\),

\[
|A_{10}|=10,\quad |A_{25}|=25,\quad |A_{10}\cap A_{25}|=\gcd(10,25)=5,
\]

so

\[
M_{10}+M_{25}\ge (10+25-5)+10=40.
\]

3. For \(A_{50}\) and \(A_{125}\),

\[
|A_{50}|=50,\quad |A_{125}|=125,\quad |A_{50}\cap A_{125}|=\gcd(50,125)=25,
\]

so

\[
M_{50}+M_{125}\ge (50+125-25)+50=200.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} M_d
=
M_1+M_2+M_5+M_{10}+M_{25}+M_{50}+M_{125}+M_{250}
\]

\[
\ge 1+8+40+200+250=499.
\]

It remains to show that \(499\) is attainable.

Let \(\varphi\) be Euler’s totient function. Choose pairwise disjoint finite sets \(B_d\) of positive integers such that \(|B_d|=\varphi(d)\) for every positive integer \(d\). For the divisors of \(250\), choose them explicitly as follows:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B_1&=\{1\},\\
B_2&=\{2\},\\
B_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
B_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
B_{25}&=\{11,12,\dots,30\},\\
B_{50}&=\{31,32,\dots,50\},\\
B_{125}&=\{51,52,\dots,150\},\\
B_{250}&=\{151,152,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For all other \(d\), choose any unused positive integers, all distinct, with \(|B_d|=\varphi(d)\).

Now define

\[
A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n} B_d.
\]

Because the \(B_d\) are disjoint and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n\), we have \(|A_n|=n\). Also, for any \(i,j\),

\[
A_i\cap A_j
=
\bigcup_{\substack{d\mid i\\ d\mid j}} B_d
=
\bigcup_{d\mid \gcd(i,j)} B_d
=
A_{\gcd(i,j)}.
\]

Hence

\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=|A_{\gcd(i,j)}|=\gcd(i,j),
\]

so the required condition holds.

For the divisors of \(250\), the maxima are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
M_1&=1,\\
M_2&=2,\\
M_5&=6,\\
M_{10}&=10,\\
M_{25}&=30,\\
M_{50}&=50,\\
M_{125}&=150,\\
M_{250}&=250.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus

\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} M_d
=
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250
=
499.
\]

Therefore the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]
